name: Information-Theoretic Surprisal Profile
description: Evaluates text using Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) and localized 'surprisal' metrics. AI text maintains a statistically flat profile of predictable transitions, whereas human text exhibits sharp spikes of high-surprisal (unexpected) word choices.
algorithm: Pointwise Mutual Information & Localized Surprisal Mapping
mechanism: In Information Theory, 'Surprisal' measures how unexpected a specific word is given its preceding context. When humans write, their cognitive process is non-linear and associative; they frequently retrieve highly unexpected vocabulary, jump between metaphors, or introduce sudden context shifts. This creates a deeply jagged 'surprisal profile' with sharp peaks of high information entropy. Large Language Models, however, generate text via autoregressive probability-smoothing. To maximize coherence and minimize error, their decoding algorithms (like nucleus sampling or beam search) heavily bias toward minimizing localized surprisal. An AI's text will ride a consistently safe, low-surprisal curve. This algorithm calculates the Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) between adjacent tokens to determine the predictability of each linguistic transition. It then graphs these values to create an Information-Theoretic Profile of the entire document. If the document displays a perfectly flat, mathematically 'safe' surprisal curve with an unnatural absence of high-entropy spikes, it is strongly flagged as probabilistically generated.
useCase: Crucial for analyzing long-form academic papers, literature, investigative journalism, and creative essays where mathematical probability curves effectively map the cognitive footprint of the author.
strengths:
• Captures the fundamental architectural limitation of all autoregressive Next-Prediction Language Models.
• Highly resilient against simple synonym replacement or light human editing, as the underlying statistical curvature (the relative distribution of surprisal) remains intact.
• Provides a purely mathematical, objective proof of generation, completely independent of grammatical or semantic content.
limitations:
• Requires significant text length (minimum 300 words) to establish a mathematical baseline and map a reliable probability curve; utterly useless on short social media posts.
• Heavily dependent on the reference corpus used for PMI calculations; if the training data of the evaluator doesn't match the domain of the text (e.g., evaluating medical text with a general English corpus), it will yield massive false positives.
• Very high computational cost compared to basic lexical density checks.
parameters:
Analysis: Autoregressive Predictability & Surprisal Profiling
Metric: Variance of Pointwise Mutual Information (Local Entropy Spikes)
Output: 0-100 Probabilistic Smoothing (Lack of Surprisal) Score
accuracy: High — 82-89% on long-form, multi-paragraph texts. It acts as a highly reliable structural audit of the text's underlying probability matrix.

references.title: Shannon, C.E. (1948). A Mathematical Theory of Communication. Bell System Technical Journal.
Mitchell, E. et al. (2023). DetectGPT: Zero-Shot Machine-Generated Text Detection using Probability Curvature. ICML.
